author: Shareholders Unite
title: Trade Tensions No Big Deal?
text:
Some people seem to think that the trade tensions on multiple fronts (albeit invariably with the US involved) are a sideshow, at least as far as the markets are concerned.
Commenting on the proposed tariffs on Chinese imports, SA contributor Ian Bezek argued:
I don't see these tariffs as a big deal.
And he quoted another SA contributor , Alan Longborn, who argued that the economic impact from these tariffs are minor compared to the size of the economies involved (China and the US) and the actions against others (EU, Mexico, Canada) are more "bluff and bluster."
Bezek adds the following:
Expect the same general development of the story, though. After Trump's big bluff, some far smaller actual action will occur. Congress is unlikely to go along with a plan that would wreck Chinese-American trade relations; too many jobs in politicians' home districts would come under fire otherwise. Trump himself has gloated numerous times on his Twitter account about how well the stock market and unemployment numbers are going during his term. It's not in his personal interest to trigger a market correction while inciting a global trade war.
And indeed, the $50B of tariffs on Chinese exports that the US imposed constitutes just 0.4% of the Chinese economy. Well, perhaps. But we give you the following to ponder about:
German car maker Daimler ( OTCPK:DDAIF ) ( OTCPK:DMLRY ) just lowered guidance (only a few months after increasing guidance), citing trade troubles. The Dow has been down for 8 days in a row (until Friday, June 22). Asian markets, Chinese ones in particular, have been tanking. Let's discuss some of these items, here is Reuters :
World shares rose on Friday but were set to end in the red for a second week running amid intensifying worries over the fallout of a trade dispute resulting from U.S. tariffs, while oil prices rose with an OPEC meeting underway.
Then there is this from CNBC :
There have been 35 moves of 1 percent or more in the Dow Jones industrial average so far this year. CNBC found fully a third of these moves, or 12 days, were linked to news about trade. On seven of the 12 days, negative trade developments sent the Dow lower by an average of 1.7 percent and cost investors a cumulative $700 billion in market capitalization. On the same days that the Dow dropped 1 percent on trade news, the S&P 500 fell a cumulative $2.2 trillion.
And most famously of course, JPMorgan's Marko Kolanovic, who tried to calculate the impact of trade tensions on the market a couple of weeks ago and concluded two weeks ago ( Business Insider ):
He estimates that US equities have already absorbed a 4.5% hit — give or take 1%. Applying that to current market capitalization, Kolanovic says this translates to $1.25 trillion of "value destruction" for US firms. For context, that's roughly two-thirds of the positive impact of fiscal measures. "A negotiation that includes bluffing/threats can be successful in a two-party negotiation setup, but is more likely to deliver self-defeating results in a complex system such as global trade," said Kolanovic.
Of course, we grant that ascribing market movements to particular motives is a rather speculative business. But on the other hand, we could still be in the very early innings of a trade war, or multiple trade wars, with all their disruptive economic effects basically yet to come.
These disruptive effects could be quite serious. The EU has already retaliated against the US tariffs on steel and aluminium, as did China and Mexico. The US isn't likely to take that lying down. Here is the NYT (our emphasis):
The European Union fought back on Friday against the Trump administration’s tariffs, slapping penalties on an array of American products that target the president’s political base, like bourbon, motorcycles and orange juice. The European counterattack on $3.2 billion of goods, a response to the administration’s measures on steel and aluminum imports, adds another front to a trade war that has engulfed allies and adversaries around the world. China and Mexico have already retaliated with their own tariffs, and Canada, Japan and Turkey are readying similar offensives. The risk of escalation is high since Mr. Trump has promised even more tariffs .
Indeed, can anyone imagine the US is going to take this lying down? Here is MarketWatch :
According to a report by Axios on Sunday, the conversation took place at the White House on April 24, during Macron’s state visit. When Macron suggested working together on trade to resolve the “China problem,” Trump reportedly said the European Union was a worse problem, and “then went on a rant about Germany and cars.”
Indeed, Trump has already been threatening to put tariffs on EU cars a number of times, most recently on June 22, here is Business Insider :
Trump had directed the Commerce Department to launch an investigation into imported autos in May, similar to the procedure that led to the steel and aluminum tariffs. While the results of that investigation are still weeks away, Trump raised the specter of tariffs on Twitter. "Based on the Tariffs and Trade Barriers long placed on the US and it great companies and workers by the European Union, if these Tariffs and Barriers are not soon broken down and removed, we will be placing a 20% Tariff on all of their cars coming into the US," Trump tweeted. "Build them here!" Trump has long been fixated on imported cars. Former Trump adviser Gary Cohn recounted a story during a recent panel in which Trump asked why all cars in the US weren't made domestically.
Well, German car manufacturers (as well as Japanese ones) are already manufacturing cars in the US. Trump does have a point as the EU (and China) charge higher tariffs on imported cars compared to the US.
However, a question like why are all US cars not made domestically is rather silly. We could just ask in the Netherlands why all films are not made in our country, or all of our cheese, etc.
The whole point of international trade is actually to expand choices for consumers and expand markets for producers, which leads to specialization, increased competition and economies of scale and scope, and a host of resulting efficiency and cost gains.
That is, it is distinctly a positive-sum game, not the zero-sum game that many observers seem to think it is ("their win is at our expense"). People might actually want to study the law of comparative advantage for starters.
Our basic fear is that part of the present US administration displays a profound lack of understanding of international trade issues, and that ill-informed facts and concepts are informing actual policy decisions, hugely increasing the risks of things going wrong.
Here are some examples (for a more thorough discussion on some of these points, see here ):
Trade is not a zero-sum game where one country's win necessarily produces a loss in another country. Having a trade deficit isn't necessarily a sign of a failing, or even weak economy; in fact, it can be a sign of a booming economy (which leads to booming demand, hence also booming demand for imports). Companies compete but countries don't. A country's standard of living depends on its own productivity, whether other countries get ahead has surprisingly little influence on that. Reducing bilateral trade deficits doesn't make any sense . The deficit will simply show up elsewhere as trade deficits are the result of a country spending more than it earns. Import tariffs are simply a tax on consumers. EU tariffs on US goods are just 3%, on average, per the US government's own Guide to Exporters . No, reducing a trade deficit doesn't increase GDP dollar for dollar, as Peter Navarro (Trump's main trade adviser) argues , which is a really basic economics 101 error and not something you'd expect from a person in his position. VAT in the EU (or elsewhere) doesn't provide the EU with a competitive advantage. No, the trade deficit isn't $800B as the President likes to claim , that's the deficit in goods only, but the US actually has a substantial surplus in services. The US government also doesn't seem to appreciate the role of international supply networks, value added and the role of its own multinational companies. Take for instance the role of American MNEs, from Bloomberg :
The U.S. has a surplus of $20 billion with China and $1.4 trillion with the rest of the world. That’s not a normal trade balance, of course, where the U.S. registered an annual deficit of more than $330 billion with China and about $550 billion with the world last year, but an "aggregate sales surplus" which measures both direct trade and the sales of multinational companies, according to research by Deutsche Bank AG.
A substantial part of world trade is simply carried out within MNEs and many of these happen to be American. Equally, the US does have a substantial trade deficit with China (even if the latter's overall trade surplus has come down from 10% of GDP to around a fairly modest 2% of GDP).
Or take value added. One of the US's main concerns seems to be the high-tech China 2025 agenda, so it's deliberating on a series of trade barriers to Chinese high-tech exports.
However, the value that the Chinese are adding to many of these high-tech exports is actually surprisingly limited. They use a lot of foreign content from highly specialist suppliers in Japan, Korea and even the US itself:
You see that the domestic content of Chinese electronics exports is below 50%, a bit higher for overall manufacturing but still much lower than US figures. Consider for instance Apple's ( AAPL ) iPhone (from CNBC ):
In the case of the Apple iPhone, this means that China's exports balance accounts for the full $500 iPhone value, when China adds only approximately $15 to $30 of the value to the phone. Most of the iPhone value accretes to Samsung in Korea ($150) and to Apple — the brand owner and engineer. This highlights how the normal accounting of trade flows is inherently distorted under the current trade-deficit estimates.
So by imposing tariffs the US not only hurts its own consumers and companies that rely on imported components, any retaliation hits the US harder as it has a much higher domestic value added component in its manufacturing exports.
We would argue that exposing itself on so many trade fronts, upsetting long-term allies and trading partners in the process, adds an additional vulnerability and increases the chances of a breakdown in the international trade system.
There are also some valid points that the US trade team makes concerning Chinese respect (or lack of it) for foreign intellectual property (although this is a fairly common problem in developing countries) and the 10% EU tariffs on imported cars, which are higher than those in the US.
But, in an excellent article, Teresa Barger, the CEO of Cartica Management (an emerging markets activist fund), argues that China is already doing much of the things the US wants it to do:
FDI flows are no longer necessarily tied to joint ventures with Chinese counterparts (which was a way to access American IP). China is already competitive in a host of high-tech industries (alternative energy, EVs, AI, etc.) and as a result, it's more interested in protecting its own IP than to steal somebody else's. And especially ( Barger ):
The United States wants China to buy more American goods and services — and so does China. Trump wants to impose stiff tariffs to prevent China from flooding the American market with increasingly less expensive technological products, like smartphones, computers and related accessories, which collectively comprise China's biggest exports to the United States. And China agrees — they want to export higher value-added goods, especially those with a high innovation content. Interests are much more aligned than either country wants to admit .
The point is, once again, does the US trade team actually understand this? We're not convinced.
Economic spillovers Are there any signs these trade conflicts are starting to have real economic effects? Well, we have already mentioned Daimler's profit warning and Kolanovic's calculations of stock market damage, but that's not all (South China Morning Post):
More Chinese companies in the US are transferring their profits back home as tensions between Washington and Beijing escalate to the threshold of an all-out trade war, according to a recent survey by a non-profit organisation representing Chinese enterprises in America... The CGCC-USA results dovetail with new data released by Rhodium Group, a consultancy that tracks investment flows between China and the US. The value of Chinese investments in the US in the first five months of 2018 dropped by 92 per cent , year-on-year, to US$1.8 billion, according to a Rhodium report published on Wednesday.
If the uncertainty is affecting the stock market and Chinese capital flows, it's likely to have already some effect on business investment and the economy. This is what the WTO argued back in April (from the FT ):
But the WTO also said it was detecting signs that rising trade tensions may already be having an impact on business confidence and investment decisions. It warned that any escalation in the sort of tit-for-tat tariff wars that the US and China have threatened in recent weeks would undermine the global recovery.
It's also what ECB Board member Benoit Coeure argued as well .
Trifecta+ What Bezek does argue is that the real danger for the markets is the Fed, and the effect of increasing interest rates on emerging markets. This is something we have warned about for quite some time , so we hardly disagree here.
There is a trifecta working against many of these emerging markets where there has been a buildup of dollar denominated private sector debt:
Rising interest rates Rising dollar Rising oil price But add to that the possibility of an economic slowdown or even recession as trade conflicts are spilling over into the real economy. But there are more feedback loops:
Tariffs increase prices, which could lead to a more aggressive Fed and a higher dollar. As trade tensions grow, the dollar is likely to become more important as a safe haven investment . Emerging markets are likely to bear the brunt. Perennial bear Edwards argued that the real problem is the US-EU trade tensions ( Business Insider ):
Edwards points out that as the Federal Reserve has become more hawkish toward monetary tightening, the European Central Bank has been more dovish in its efforts to taper asset purchases. The resulting divergence has led to a weak euro and a strong dollar, which in turn has allowed the eurozone's trade surplus to grow because a depressed currency makes exports more attractive. Edwards says a trade war is primed to break out as a result — and could dwarf the escalating trade conflict with China.
Emerging markets are very vulnerable should trade tensions escalate, here is the FT :
“The generalised view [about trade tensions] is that if the world is risk-off, you’re not going to buy an EM country,” said Alan Ruskin at Deutsche Bank. Trade tensions could also lead to the US inflicting “an awful lot of harm, particularly to countries where trade is lopsided”, such as China and Germany.
So trade tensions and a potential EM crisis can't really be seen in isolation, in our view.
Conclusion We don't think trade is a sideshow. Negative effects are already being felt on the stock market; they're clouding investment decisions as they increase uncertainty, and they have produced a retreat of Chinese money from the US.
Emerging markets, quite a few of which are already under considerable strain with the rise in US interest rates and the dollar, are very vulnerable to escalating trade tensions; these clearly aren't a sideshow for emerging market landscape.
Disclosure: I/we have no positions in any stocks mentioned, and no plans to initiate any positions within the next 72 hours.
I wrote this article myself, and it expresses my own opinions. I am not receiving compensation for it (other than from Seeking Alpha). I have no business relationship with any company whose stock is mentioned in this article.
